# Goal

We will make two figures:

1. a barplot showing microbiome composition; and
2. a beta-diversity plot showing which samples have similar communities.

# 1. Choose your files

The abundance table and the sample sheet are already in the folder folder. Call their filenames here for later read-in.

```{r files}

abundance_file <- "abundance_table_species_CLEAN.tsv"
metadata_file  <- "sample_sheet_biol351_flygut_CLEAN.csv"

```

# 2. Load packages

```{r packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(tidyverse)
library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)

```

These packages should be pre-installed, ask your instructor for help if you have any issues loading them.

# 3. Import the data

Run this chunk without changing it. It combines the abundance table, taxonomy, and sample information into one `phyloseq` object.

```{r import, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Read the EPI2ME abundance table
abundance <- read_tsv(abundance_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

# Remove the taxonomy and total-count columns, leaving only
# the read counts: taxa are rows and samples are columns
counts <- abundance %>% select(-tax, -total) %>% as.matrix()

# Use each taxon's full taxonomy string as its row name.
# make.unique() prevents errors if two taxa have the same name.
rownames(counts) <- make.unique(abundance$tax)

# Split the taxonomy into ranks
taxonomy <- stringr::str_split_fixed(abundance$tax, ";", 8)
colnames(taxonomy) <- c("Domain", "Kingdom", "Phylum", "Class", "Order", "Family", "Genus", "Species")
rownames(taxonomy) <- rownames(counts)

# Read the sample sheet
metadata <- read_csv(metadata_file, show_col_types = FALSE) %>% as.data.frame()

rownames(metadata) <- metadata$alias
# Keep only samples found in the abundance table and put them in the same order
metadata <- metadata[colnames(counts), ]

# Set the order of the four experimental groups in plots and output
metadata$Group <- factor(
  metadata$Group,
  levels = c(
    "Control_Sedentary",
    "Control_Exercise",
    "Obese_Sedentary",
    "Obese_Exercise"
  )
)

# Combine everything into a phyloseq object
ps <- phyloseq(
  otu_table(counts, taxa_are_rows = TRUE),
  tax_table(taxonomy),
  sample_data(metadata)
)

# Remove taxa with no reads in the analyzed samples
ps <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(ps) > 0, ps)

# Convert read counts to relative abundance
ps_relative <- transform_sample_counts(ps, function(x) x / sum(x))

```

# 4. Compositional barplot

Each color represents one of the most abundant bacterial taxa. All remaining taxa are combined as **Other**, so every bar still adds up to 100%.

```{r barplot, fig.width=14, fig.height=6}

# Choose how many taxa to list separately
number_to_show <- 10

# FIRST GLOM:
# Combine all taxa belonging to the same genus
ps_tax <- tax_glom(ps_relative, taxrank = "Genus")

# Identify the 10 most abundant genera across all samples
top_tax_ids <- names(
  sort(taxa_sums(ps_tax), decreasing = TRUE)
)[1:number_to_show]

# Rename each genus outside the top 10 as "Other"
tax_table(ps_tax)[
  !taxa_names(ps_tax) %in% top_tax_ids,
  "Genus"
] <- "Other"

# SECOND GLOM:
# Combine all the genera now labeled "Other" into one category
ps_tax <- tax_glom(ps_tax, taxrank = "Genus")

# Make the barplot
plot_bar(ps_tax, x = "Sample", fill = "Genus") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Paired") +
  facet_grid(. ~ Group, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Relative abundance", fill = "Genus") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 7))

```

# 5. Beta diversity

Samples plotted closer together have more similar microbiome compositions.

```{r beta-diversity, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}

# Calculate Bray-Curtis differences among samples
bray_pcoa <- ordinate(ps_relative, method = "PCoA", distance = "bray")

# Colorblind-friendly Okabe-Ito colors for the four groups
group_colors <- c(
  "Control_Sedentary" = "#56B4E9",
  "Control_Exercise" = "#009E73",
  "Obese_Sedentary" = "#F0E442",
  "Obese_Exercise" = "#E69F00"
)

# Plot the samples and color them by experimental group
plot_ordination(ps_relative, bray_pcoa, color = "Group") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = Group), level = 0.95) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = group_colors) +
  theme_classic()

```

# 6. PERMANOVA

PERMANOVA tests whether microbiome composition differs among the four experimental groups.

```{r permanova}

# Use the same Bray-Curtis differences as the PCoA
bray_distance <- distance(ps_relative, method = "bray")
sample_info <- data.frame(sample_data(ps_relative))

# Test for a difference among the four experimental groups
set.seed(123)
permanova <- adonis2(
  bray_distance ~ Group,
  data = sample_info,
  permutations = 999
)

permanova

```

In the `Group` row:

- `Pr(>F)` is the p-value. A value below 0.05 provides evidence that at least one of the four groups differs in overall microbiome composition.
- `R2` is the proportion of variation associated with experimental group.

For this introductory activity, we will treat this as a simple test of group differences. A more complete analysis would also check whether the groups have similar within-group dispersion.

# Questions

1. Which bacterial taxa are most abundant?
2. How do the compositional profiles differ among the four experimental groups?
3. Do samples from the same experimental group cluster together on the beta-diversity plot?
4. What does it mean when two samples are far apart?
5. What are the PERMANOVA p-value and R2? What do they suggest?
